To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) CNN can be trained on crowd data, (2) the choice of aggregation affects the accuracy, (3) CNN trained on crowd data performs worse than on ground-truth, but better than random forest, and (4) AggNet improves the accuracy of the CNN trained on crowds.
1) Deep CNN learning from crowd-based annotations is feasible, and 2) the choice of aggregation method and the number of annotators are crucial factors for the success of learning from crowd.
1) Deep learning from crowds is feasible and 2) the proposed crowdsourcing layer (aggnet) is a valuable tool for training CNN on crowd-based data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new concept for training CNNs from crowdsourcing and the study of different annotation strategies for the biomedical domain.
the following questions: How to learn from crowds?
the following contributions: a) We propose a new concept for deep learning from crowds by introducing the AggNet, a crowdsourcing layer for aggregating noisy data collected from crowds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
deep CNN can learn to detect objects from crowdsourcing data, but only if a suitable aggregation method is used.
deep learning from crowdsourcing can be a valuable source of training data for deep CNN, but it needs to be carefully designed and implemented.
AggNet is a promising approach for learning from crowds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
deep learning from crowd can be a promising solution to the lack of annotated data for biomedical imaging applications.
AggNet can be used as a tool for training deep CNN on crowd-based datasets, and can be applied to other medical imaging applications.
deep learning from crowd annotations is possible and can be achieved by integrating data aggregation directly as a part of the CNN learning process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AggNet is able to learn from noisy annotations and achieve a comparable performance to the state of the art on the task of detecting mitosis in breast cancer histology images.
deep CNNs are able to learn from crowds, and that the aggregation of noisy annotations from crowdsourcing is a key step in order to obtain accurate results.
deep CNNs can be trained on crowdsourced data with a significant accuracy.
